sections.h2: Who records deeds in Santa Cruz County
sections.html:
A single office, the Santa Cruz County Recorder, handles recording countywide. Deeds, mortgages, maps and surveys all pass through it, and voter registration lives there too. Each accepted document is given a docket and page number, indexed and microfilmed. The Recorder page offers searchable documents beginning with 1984. Call 520-375-7990 or write to recorder@santacruzcountyaz.gov with questions.

Nogales is the county seat, yet a house in Rio Rico, Tubac, Sonoita or Patagonia is recorded through the very same office, with identical rules.

sections.h2: What a deed must look like
sections.html:
Arizona spells out the format in ARS 11-480. A document that misses one of the listed conditions can be turned away at the counter, so run through this list before sending anything.

  • A caption naming the document, such as warranty deed or release of mortgage.
  • A legible original carrying original signatures, unless the law allows otherwise.
  • For anything signed from January 1, 1991 forward, paper up to 8.5 by 14 inches and print no smaller than ten point.
  • A half-inch margin on every side, plus a top margin of at least two inches on page one, which the Recorder saves for its stamps.
  • For an instrument that amends an earlier recorded document, the earlier document's recording date, docket and page.

If you want the recorded original mailed back, a return address fits in the left three and one-half inches of that top strip. The Recorder also points filers to the exemption codes in ARS 11-1134.

sections.h2: Affidavit of legal value and exempt deeds
sections.html:
A deed moving title, or a sales contract, has to come with an affidavit of legal value. Buyer and seller sign it, or an agent signs for them. The form, built on ARS 11-1133, asks for both parties' names and addresses, the legal description and parcel number, and the date of sale. It also wants the total consideration, how the purchase is financed, whether personal property is five percent or more of the price, and whether a house will be lived in by its owner or rented out. A deed that arrives without a complete affidavit gets refused, unless it carries a notation of an exemption.

The exemption list in ARS 11-1134 reaches many family and entity transfers. Gifts, court-ordered conveyances, quitclaims made for no money, trustee's deeds sold under a power of sale, and corrective deeds all qualify. So do house transfers for nominal consideration among spouses, parents and children, grandparents and grandchildren, or siblings. Whichever applies must be written on the face of the deed at recording. A title company can match your situation to the right code.

The base charge is $30 for each instrument. If the United States, Arizona or a political subdivision is a party and requests the recording, the charge is $15. Everything else follows the county schedule. Phone the Recorder before you mail a check to be sure the amounts haven't changed.

Ask for copies by email and pay in advance. A map no bigger than 8.5 by 14 inches can be recorded like any other document at the standard fee.

sections.h2: Is there a transfer tax on a home sale?
sections.html:
Arizona charges a flat real estate transfer fee of $2 per deed or contract, collected before recording. Under ARS 11-1132 that $2 is folded into the $30 standard fee, so it adds nothing on top. A county can also add a document storage surcharge of up to $4 per instrument, and that amount sits inside the $30 as well.

On the affidavit, "value" is the full actual consideration paid or still to be paid, with any liens counted in. If the deed is a gift or carries only nominal consideration, value becomes the estimated open-market price. A title company can confirm whether your deed owes anything further.

Anyone walking a document in must usually produce valid photo identification, as ARS 11-472 requires. The rule applies at the Recorder's office and at any recording kiosk. Individuals can show a driver's license or state ID, a passport or passport card, a U.S. military ID or a tribal ID.

Documents submitted by these filers are exempt: escrow officers and offices, title insurance agents and insurers, state or federally chartered banks and credit unions, active members of the State Bar of Arizona, and government entities. Exempt filers can show items like a bar card with a government ID, an employee badge or a company letter. The Recorder writes down the ID type, name and number but keeps no copy, and that information isn't a public record.

Card payments are taken at the counter or by phone on weekdays between 8 a.m. and 5 p.m., Arizona time. A payment of $0 to $60 on a Visa, Mastercard or Discover credit card adds a flat $1.50. Visa Signature Debit adds a flat $3.95. Payments of $61 and up add 2.49 percent. The Recorder keeps none of the surcharge.

Housing in the county totals 20,135 units, with owners in 69.3 percent of them and a median owner-occupied value of $233,000 for 2020 to 2024.

• Confirm the deed has a caption, an original signature and the two-inch top margin.
  • Sign the affidavit of legal value, or have an exemption noted on the face of the deed.
  • Let the title or escrow company file, since they skip the in-person ID rule.
  • Call the Recorder to confirm the fee, and the Treasurer for any tax balance, before closing.

When the buyer is a company, ask who will present the deed. Recorder staff can explain the format rules but can't give legal advice. A cash buyer who skips a lender also skips the loan documents, which leaves the deed as the main paper to record.

After recording, the deed gets its docket and page number and enters the index, and the original comes back to the return address. Keep that copy with your closing papers. If something is rejected at the counter, the usual causes are a missing caption, a short top margin, an unsigned affidavit or no exemption note. Fix the one item, and the filing can be presented again.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to record a deed in Santa Cruz County?
faqs.a: Thirty dollars covers each ordinary instrument, and fifteen dollars covers one with a government party. Copies run $1 a page; a certified copy costs $3 plus $1 a page. Phone the Recorder for the latest amounts.

faqs.q: Is there a transfer tax in Santa Cruz County?
faqs.a: Arizona sets a flat $2 real estate transfer fee per deed or contract, and it is included in the $30 recording fee. Ask the Recorder or your title company whether any other charge applies.

faqs.q: Do I need an affidavit of legal value to record a deed?
faqs.a: Usually yes. A deed or sales contract must carry a completed affidavit signed by buyer and seller or their agents, unless the instrument notes an ARS 11-1134 exemption such as a deed of gift or a court-ordered conveyance.

faqs.q: Who is exempt from the photo ID rule for in-person recording?
faqs.a: Escrow offices, title insurers and their agents, chartered banks and credit unions, active State Bar of Arizona members and government bodies get a pass. Anybody else filing in person needs valid photo ID.

faqs.q: How do I reach the Santa Cruz County Recorder?
faqs.a: Dial 520-375-7990 or write to recorder@santacruzcountyaz.gov. Phone card payments are accepted on weekdays from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. Searchable records start with 1984.
